title: Net-electric fusion using a low-neutron fuel cycle

concept.text: The innovation would be an integrated fusion plant that exports more electricity than it consumes while using a fuel cycle that produces substantially fewer neutrons than deuterium–tritium fusion. Proton–boron-11 is the principal example supported by the supplied evidence: its primary fusion reaction produces three energetic helium ions, which are charged particles. The intended advance combines useful electrical output with a different fuel and radiation regime; observing individual fusion reactions would not establish it.

Low neutron production would not mean radiation-free operation. Secondary reactions can produce neutrons, and the plasma emits electromagnetic radiation through bremsstrahlung, the radiation generated when electrons are deflected by charged particles. The complete plant would need to turn fusion energy into electricity while covering the energy required to create and maintain the reacting fuel and operate its supporting systems. Direct conversion of charged-particle energy could be an option, but the concept does not require it: thermal energy conversion is also compatible with the net-electric goal.

Scope synthesis: the concept retains its broader identity as net-electric fusion using a low-neutron fuel cycle. The supplied research supports detailed discussion of proton–boron-11 specifically; it does not establish that every other proposed low-neutron fuel shares the same reaction conditions, losses, residual neutron production or engineering advantages.

significance.text: If achieved, this would establish a distinct fusion engineering capability: useful electrical generation with substantially reduced neutron production. Lower neutron exposure could ease some component damage and material activation, potentially reducing the associated replacement and maintenance burden. These are conditional engineering consequences, not measured benefits from an operating plant. The theoretical proton–boron-11 inertial-fusion analysis describes residual neutron production as orders of magnitude below deuterium–tritium production, but that comparison is not a demonstrated whole-plant radiation inventory.

A proton–boron-11 plant would not require tritium as its primary fusion fuel and could therefore avoid the breeding requirement associated with supplying that primary fuel. This implication follows from the particular fuel choice; reducing neutron production alone does not establish the same benefit for every proposed fuel cycle. The charged helium products also create a possible route to direct energy conversion, although a practical conversion system and its contribution to net output would still need demonstration.

The prospective advantage has important limits. Fewer neutrons would not eliminate secondary neutron reactions, other radiation or all activated materials. Neither the reaction measurement nor the theoretical analysis establishes that such a plant would be compact, inexpensive or economically competitive. Any downstream benefit from easier maintenance or a different power-conversion system would depend on overcoming the demanding plasma conditions and energy losses without introducing greater burdens elsewhere.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is sustained plant-level net electrical production from a low-neutron fusion fuel. For proton–boron-11, producing reactions is only an initial step. A productive plasma must generate enough fusion energy to overcome losses and the energy cost of maintaining the reacting conditions, with sufficient energy remaining after conversion to electricity to cover plant consumption. Plasma energy gain and electrical reactor breakeven are different milestones because input and output conversion efficiencies affect the latter.

Bremsstrahlung is a major barrier because energy carried away as radiation can undermine the energy balance needed for a productive burn. The January 2026 analysis examines emission and reabsorption in proton–boron-11 inertial fusion and also discusses demanding burn conditions and helium-ash poisoning, in which accumulated reaction products impair the reacting plasma. These are interacting constraints on maintaining useful fusion output, rather than a single obstacle resolved by detecting more reactions.

The theoretical conclusions require careful boundaries. The 2026 paper concerns inertial fusion and uses substantial model assumptions; the review identifies uncertainty and model breakdown in the most optimistic dense, partly degenerate regime. It therefore provides evidence of serious constraints, not a universal impossibility proof for all proton–boron-11 configurations or all low-neutron fuels. Conversely, uncertainty in that regime does not establish a workable route to net power.

Engineering synthesis: the remaining work also includes integrating fuel handling, plasma operation, energy conversion and maintainable components into a system with a positive electrical balance. Its low-neutron advantage would need verification through the radiation produced by the actual operating system, including secondary reactions and resulting activation. These are proposed plant-level requirements extending beyond the reaction and modeling results in the supplied evidence.

current_state.text: A March 2023 National Institute for Fusion Science report describes measurements of proton–boron-11 fusion in a magnetically confined plasma in the Large Helical Device, involving NIFS and TAE Technologies. It reports detection of energetic helium produced by the reaction and identifies the corresponding work by R. M. Magee, K. Ogawa and colleagues as published in Nature Communications on February 21, 2023. This demonstrated fusion reactions and detection of their products; it did not demonstrate net electrical generation or an integrated power plant.

The primary proton–boron-11 reaction produces three energetic helium ions. Descriptions of that primary reaction as neutron-free must be distinguished from the radiation produced by a complete reacting system. The 2026 theoretical paper identifies a neutron-producing helium–boron secondary reaction chain in inertial fusion and concludes that residual neutron production remains, even though it is substantially below that of deuterium–tritium fusion. This is a theoretical result for the analyzed setting, not a measured neutron yield for a working power plant.

Ian E. Ochs, Elijah J. Kolmes, Alexander S. Glasser and Nathaniel J. Fisch’s “Bremsstrahlung constraints on proton-boron 11 inertial fusion,” published in Physics of Plasmas on January 8, 2026, uses burn simulations incorporating bremsstrahlung emission and reabsorption to examine conditions for energy production. It identifies radiation losses as a major constraint. The supplied review identifies it as a published theoretical article, not a preprint or experimental demonstration, and emphasizes its simplifying assumptions and uncertainty in dense, partly degenerate conditions.

Evidence boundary: the supplied review assessed the complete institutional report and the full theoretical article, with no extraction truncation reported. The 2023 experimental account is therefore grounded here in the institutional report rather than direct review of the Nature Communications research article. Earlier research text says the Nature publisher page failed to open, but the supplied review found no record confirming that failure. The theoretical paper’s qualitative claims were assessed from its prose without inspection of the plotted figures.

Coverage limitation: these supplied findings do not document an integrated low-neutron net-electric plant. They also do not establish an exhaustive field status as of November 2026, because the supplied freshness record is empty. The absence of such a demonstration from this evidence set should not be treated as proof that every later or otherwise unreviewed claim is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate an integrated low-neutron-fuel plant with sustained, measured net electrical export over a declared accounting boundary. Report electrical generation and all energy inputs needed for operation, including fuel preparation, plasma heating or compression, conversion losses and supporting systems. Account explicitly for startup energy and any change in stored energy so that discharge of previously supplied energy cannot be mistaken for net generation. The paper’s distinction between plasma gain and reactor breakeven motivates this requirement; the detailed accounting proposal is not an established acceptance standard.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed radiation demonstration: measure neutron production, its energy distribution and material activation under the same operating conditions used to establish electrical export. Include secondary reactions and compare with deuterium–tritium fusion using a declared normalization, such as useful electrical output. Specify in advance what reduction would justify the low-neutron designation. The supplied theoretical discussion motivates assessing residual neutrons, but it does not supply a universal plant-level threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed radiation demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical demonstration: establish a maintainable fuel and power-conversion system through repeated operation, documenting consumables, helium-ash management, component degradation, replacement needs and recovery after shutdown. If direct charged-particle conversion is claimed as a central advantage, demonstrate its efficiency and contribution within the integrated energy balance. Otherwise, a thermal conversion route could satisfy the concept if the complete plant exports net electricity.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed practical demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries: use independently checked diagnostics and repeat the result across a declared range of operating conditions. Set demonstration duration, repetition requirements, maintenance allowances and acceptable neutron production before testing; the supplied evidence does not establish numerical thresholds for them. Finite demonstrations would establish the breadth and duration actually tested, while longer-term availability, economics and transfer to other fuels or configurations would remain separate questions.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NUC-01, “A self-sustaining, net-electric fusion power plant,” shares the general goal of useful fusion electricity. NUC-07 adds the particular requirement of a low-neutron fuel cycle and its associated fuel, radiation and energy-conversion regime. Only NUC-01’s title is supplied, so this comparison establishes a broad relationship rather than a verified detailed boundary between their full specifications.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-06, “Reactor structural materials that remain reliable under extreme neutron exposure,” addresses material tolerance to neutron damage; NUC-07 seeks to reduce the neutron burden through fuel choice. Reduced exposure could ease some material demands without eliminating them. NUC-11, “Durable materials and chemistry control for aggressive reactor coolants,” concerns a separate materials and coolant challenge that could remain relevant depending on the eventual plant design.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-02, “Mass-produced fission plants with radically lower delivered cost,” and NUC-10, “Long-lived, low-intervention nuclear power for remote sites,” concern cost, deployment and operational outcomes. Achieving NUC-07 would not by itself demonstrate mass production, low delivered cost or remote-site reliability. NUC-04, “High-power nuclear propulsion for routine deep-space missions,” would additionally require a suitable propulsion system and mission-level performance; net-electric low-neutron fusion alone would not establish those capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-03, “A scalable closed fuel cycle that consumes most long-lived actinides,” and NUC-09, “Very-high-burnup fuel with robust fission-product retention,” address actinides and fission-fuel behavior. They remain distinct from the proton–boron-11 fusion regime examined here. NUC-13, “A fuel cycle with substantially stronger built-in proliferation resistance,” concerns another fuel-cycle property that cannot be inferred solely from lower neutron production or the absence of tritium as the primary fuel.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-05, “Practical remote verification of otherwise inaccessible operating reactors,” and NUC-12, “Reliable, non-invasive, real-time three-dimensional reactor-core diagnosis,” concern observation and verification capabilities. NUC-07 would require credible measurements of its own performance, but that requirement does not establish either specialized capability. NUC-08, “Broadly applicable passive shutdown and long-term reactor cooling,” likewise addresses a separate safety and cooling capability whose applicability would require assessment for the chosen fusion design.

change_log.change: Preserved NUC-07’s identity while concentrating detailed scientific claims on proton–boron-11.
change_log.reason: The evidence supports that fuel specifically and does not establish equivalent constraints or benefits for unspecified other low-neutron fuels.

change_log.change: Separated primary charged-particle production from secondary neutron production and bremsstrahlung radiation.
change_log.reason: Neutron-free language about the primary reaction does not describe the complete reacting system or plant.

change_log.change: Tied avoidance of primary-fuel tritium breeding specifically to proton–boron-11 and retained conditional material benefits.
change_log.reason: Fuel choice supports the tritium inference; lower neutron production alone does not establish it for every fuel. Plant-level damage and activation benefits have not been demonstrated in the supplied evidence.

change_log.change: Expanded the 2023 result with its publication date, experimental setting and reaction-product scope.
change_log.reason: The institutional report supports a meaningful reaction measurement, which must remain distinct from net power or an integrated plant demonstration.

change_log.change: Expanded the January 2026 theoretical finding with emission and reabsorption, helium ash, conversion efficiencies and model limitations.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain the barriers while avoiding an unsupported universal impossibility conclusion.

change_log.change: Qualified the claimed Nature-page access failure and identified the actual evidence reviewed.
change_log.reason: The institutional report was reviewed, but no supplied failed-access record verifies the earlier access-failure assertion. Full text extraction also does not imply inspection of plotted figures.

change_log.change: Replaced an implied comprehensive current-status assessment with an explicit coverage limitation.
change_log.reason: The empty freshness record prevents the dated sources from establishing exhaustive field status in November 2026.

change_log.change: Developed completion criteria into explicit proposals for energy accounting, radiation assessment, maintainability and reproducibility, while retaining optional direct conversion.
change_log.reason: These make the intended breakthrough assessable without presenting proposed requirements as consensus standards or achieved results.

change_log.change: Explained relationships across the supplied roster using titles and clearly labeled synthesis.
change_log.reason: The roster supports broad distinctions, but the other concepts’ detailed specifications were not supplied.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether later or unreviewed work changes the field’s status as of November 2026.
The Nature Communications research article was not directly assessed in the supplied review, and the claimed publisher-page access failure remains unverified.
The most optimistic dense, partly degenerate regimes remain uncertain within the 2026 model; the supplied evidence does not resolve their practical feasibility.
Equivalent feasibility, radiation and fuel-handling claims for other proposed low-neutron fuels require fuel-specific evidence.
Demonstration duration, accounting boundaries, acceptable neutron production, maintenance allowances and reproducibility requirements remain to be specified.
Complete-plant electrical performance, neutron yield, activation, component lifetime and economic viability are not demonstrated by the supplied sources.
Detailed overlap with the other roster entries remains uncertain because only their IDs and titles were supplied.
